text: This is how we implemented this at our company: - We have 2 sources of data that we must backup to continue existing as a business; our postgres and binary files in S3. Everything else is derivable (elasticsearch, so on). - For postgres, we use barman. With the help of opus/fable, you can get a streaming replication backup working in no time. We have one into another server in the same datacenter (we use baremetal) and another one in another server in a different datacenter. - We then have a last resort barman backup with bi-weekly base backups + WAL streaming to S3 (both the base backup and WALs). It sends these backups + wal segments into an specific S3 bucket that has object lock in compliance mode. This is a feature from AWS S3 that even the most privileged account credentials (super admin) can't turn off nor delete the files before the object lock, which is 10 days in our case. Object lock compliance mode can only be extended, never shortened. - For S3, we store them into another versioned bucket, with lifecycle rules to also expire non current versions (== deleted objects) after 10 days. No point in object lock compliance here because it would only protect objects for the most recent 10 days, and you gain nothing. What we do instead: the app servers only have access to these bucket tru an IAM credential that can't delete old versions (so deleted objects have to expire manually via the lifecycle rule) AND this IAM credentials also can't change the object policy. IMHO, this protects us enough so that even in the worst case scenario (ransomware) we have 10 days to sort everything out and recover our AWS access. And yes, we test the S3 barman restoration and it works fine. Data loss is at max 5 minutes due to the archive_timeout=300s on the primary. For the streaming replications in the two servers I mentioned, it's less <1ms, but those wouldn't protect us much in the case of the ransomware - even tough we use tailscale and one compromised server can't ssh into the other.

text: Privacy is when nobody is looking, whether that's because they cannot look or because there's nobody that looks. Security is the former: actively denying someone or something the ability to look in a situation where they are trying. GrapheneOS does that by encouraging a locked bootloader (preventing physical attacks) and letting you deny sensor access (preventing malicious apps from accessing unnecessary info), for example. I think we agree so far? But you can also have privacy by just not installing apps that violate your privacy. Such a device could be as open as any Linux laptop where you log in with root:root. It lets you do whatever you want and access whatever you want. It's yours through and through. That's freedom without security, which may or may not have privacy depending on who you let look: if you leave it unattended at a hacker conference or have sshd with password login enabled, yeah that won't stay private for very long. But that's your choice right? You can just not invite anyone in or, in this example, bring it to someone who would do something malicious An official GrapheneOS release has a lot of features baked in against actively malicious actors (be it apps or people at border checks), but users need to work within the boundaries and limitations of the sandpit that's provided to them. They're not granted much freedom, and that limits what privacy measures you can enact. Making a backup of /data, modifying firewall or traffic routing rules, signature spoofing to substitute an untrusted app with a trusted implementation, intercepting and faking Android API responses... a lot of things are off-limits: you don't have the freedom to shape the environment to suit your needs, for example to create privacy or security The axes (privacy, freedom, security) all influence each other, but they are still separate enough that you can have one or two without the other. I can see what you mean if you say that your threat actors are skilled exploit developers and you can't have privacy without also thwarting these constant attempts. (Paranoid as that may sound, I'm sure it's true for some people.) Most people would gain more privacy from doing something about the pervasive adtech than about exploit developers they're not likely to run into. For them, LineageOS could be more private and provide more freedom while being less secure in some ways (e.g. they need to watch out which processes they grant access, for example something claiming to be backup software that turns out to be ransomware) and more secure in others (e.g. data availability by getting to make backups)

Reiterating student privacy concerns: I don't love the aggregation of data to a single company either, but the example of "every message students sent to professors and you sent back, through campus, was part of the deal" is yet another instance of "you don't have privacy when you are communicating with faculty." Universities just need to step up the privacy demands they negotiate into their contracts with LMS providers. This is not an inherent issue with the technology. Also, the fact that Canvas is owned by private equity is irrelevant. Every Ivy League school is "private equity." 5: Canvas encourages student grade obsession: This has to be the most ridiculously coddling and infantilizing claim of them all. Isn't it also true that every LMS out there allows customization of how grades are delivered, or allows you to not use that functionality at all? The crazy part of this critique is that Canvas is still an open source LMS product. Universities can self-host it and avoid points 3 and 4 and keep data entirely within the walls of the university as well as customize it however they'd like. Simon Fraser University and National Taiwan University do exactly that. I realize that essentially no significantly sized US school bothers to do that, but it is an option. And as the marketshare chart points out, one of the big three is moodle, which is more frequently self-hosted and is open source. So, again, I think this article is placing blame at the wrong place. I think a critique of Instructure the company and Canvas seems warranted, but that's less than half of what this article is doing if you ask me, it's critiquing the LMS as a concept. That is where I take major issue with what this article is doing. The final piece that makes me a little peeved at this article is that it doesn't mention the alternative to having LMS in our world, which is less access to education. A dictatorial march back to "the old days" of pen and paper and traditional learning means less access to education. It would mean that people with busy schedules, childcare obligations, people who work nights and odd hours, people with transportation challenges, etc, can't make it to school. My last degree was 100% online. I don't know how it would have worked without an LMS involved. Did I learn less effectively than someone in person with a pen and paper? text: Indeed, taxation today and historically is not based on mass surveillance and doesn't depend on mass surveillance. If you're failing to pay taxes on any scale you're going to get caught by whistleblowers or by conspicuous visible purchases. Enforcement isn't 100%, of course, but it never is for any crime and it doesn't need to be. Even if your effective tax rate is 50% evasion can only double your money at best, and you've only got taxes to pay if you've got a successful income stream-- it doesn't take much threat of imprisonment or large fines to keep someone with something to lose staying within the lines.  You're already making good money (if you're not-- no taxes) so why risk your good situation for a small constant factor more? Some amount of successful evasion simply means somewhat higher taxes for everyone else, and that is a reasonable compromise for not living in a panopticon-- particularly since no amount of surveillance can entirely prevent tax evasion. To the extent that someone wants to engage in evasion they'd route around this surveillance system or not even worry about it: Data isn't intelligence, visible income can be offset by fake expenses (which are private in this system too!)-- and so it can't be said that this scheme's surveillance would even be particularly effective at blocking tax evasion.  You'd be left with detecting it via traditional means, just as you already can even with completely private transactions, but without the privacy loss. So it's a non-solution to a non-problem, that create significant privacy related collateral harm.  It can do both because non-evaders won't bother to take the additional steps to protect themselves, and are exposed to every hack, leak, data-breach, change of policy, or abuse of lawful process. (Analog: run strong encryption or strong encryption+steganography inside key-escrowed encryption. This possibility bounds the potential benefits of key escrow but fails to bound the harms.) For any system one should imagine the abuse potential should the currently benign regime be replaced with a future genocidal one.  Certainly Germans should be well acquainted with the value of that kind of reasoning-- it isn't like targeting sub-populations for asset seizure is a hypothetical threat.  A key property of privacy loss is that it's forever: you might not mind a piece of exposure today but years from now it could turn fatal. But even then I wouldn't complain about it except for the misleading presentation of it as a privacy system and the smearing of opponents as tax evaders. It's simply a falsehood to claim people opposed to this are opposed to taxation.  Personally, I find taxation to often be a superior choice to fund public infrastructure compared to the most obvious alternatives such as printing money or accumulating debt-- particularly because taxation is more visible and thus more accountable.  But we must take great care to mitigate the potential collateral damage of taxation including accounting overhead, market distortion, and loss of privacy. The false and defamatory characterization of opponents as tax protesters is part of why I feel comfortable saying that I believe the mischaracterization of the system as 'private' is an act of intentional fraud. An honest system doesn't need to discourage or suppress its critics by falsely accusing them of being in favor of crime or other anti-social conduct.

So in that sense, we will get back to "how we were writing code in 2019" — using tools to help our own brains create. 2. The now-long history of the internet has proven to us that those skeptical of trust in what is on the other end has largely proven out. Not commercially — we can almost entirely trust what is on the other end of a business transaction, at least when trading with large players in the economy. Some costs there include compromised online identity and compromised financials (from repeated, rampant data breaches). But we can't trust the voice of individuals anymore, as proven by our rapidly disintegrating democratic norms. We are in a crisis point as a civilization when it comes to not actually talking to each other at a human level anymore, rather being mediated by the internet. So that's where that — the internet never going away — landed. I think the jury is still out on whether the internet is good for humanity. I'm not saying it will ever go away — it can't possibly — but the fact that we've accepted it as inevitable has led to us failing at considering possibilities for reigning some things in or keeping some things offline. As a present example, we now purport to trust closed models run by trillion dollar companies, when one poll showed one in five voters asking chatbots who to vote for in a few weeks in the US elections — no chance for corruption there! "How we were writing code in 2019" was being aware of where the code and algorithms we were using came from and (even in the worst case, of secreting code into a large codebase via theft) trusting it as doing as its author, a human, intended. 3. Like other cycles, unsustainable economics are propped up right now by institutional investors riding numbers-go-up until the train crashes, always looking and finding someone else to point out and say "but they're still onboard" — just like past cycles. The common person / worker / individual will be left holding the bag in very painful market convulsions that will forever scar those who actually make it. There's a cost there — ruined lives, careers, potential — a cost that we repeatedly decide is acceptable. "How we were writing code in 2019" was weighing the tradeoffs of using a product or voting with our money on its sustainability, rather than determining the future laid out by us (not at all by random or by merit) is inevitable and "the way" that we should pursue. Groupthink at its worst. I am using "How we were writing code in 2019" here not as a point that we should return to, but as the point before the hype took hold and all reason was thrown out the window and a point to consider as we weigh — really weigh — the pros and cons. Lastly, on a personal note, I've got no fear of being replaced. Like another in this subthread, I happened into a career that paid well for doing something I already loved. At times in my career, I even chose the path that made the least sense financially, in order to pursue something I loved and that satisfied my curiosities. A breach of a Defense Manpower Data Center information system exposed personal information belonging to more than 3 mn people with ties to the U.S. military. The records included names, contact details, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, military job information and other personal data.     The breach affected about 2.76 mn living individuals and another 294,000 people who are deceased, according to a Pentagon official.

The specific information exposed differs by person, and officials said they have found no evidence so far that the data has been misused.
Unauthorized users accessed DMDC system for nearly a year A small number of unauthorized users had access to the information between October 2025 and July 2026. A breach notice sent to one affected individual said DMDC discovered a security vulnerability in a file-sharing system on July 16 and immediately patched it.     The exposed information was stored without encryption, according to the Pentagon official. DMDC said it started privacy and cybersecurity incident response procedures after discovering the incident and is assessing additional measures for the affected system.

The Pentagon hasn’t disclosed who accessed the records or whether the intrusion was intentional. Officials also haven’t specified whether the affected individuals belong to a particular segment of the military community or explained why the personal information was stored on an unencrypted system.
DMDC holds more than 60 mn military-related records The Defense Manpower Data Center manages identity verification for Department of Defense ID card holders and maintains more than 60 mn personnel records.     Its databases contain information covering troops and veterans, current and former civilian employees, contractors and military family members.

The scale of DMDC’s records makes the breach considerably larger than the number of people whose data was exposed. Pentagon officials have identified roughly 3.05 mn living and deceased individuals affected by the incident, compared with more than 60 mn records maintained by the organization.
Affected individuals receive 12 months of credit monitoring The Defense Department is notifying people affected by the breach. IDX, a data breach and recovery services provider, will offer 12 months of credit monitoring to those whose information was involved.     DMDC has also been working during 2026 to correct records for hundreds of thousands of service members whose files lacked documentation required for Common Access Cards.

A Pentagon official previously said there was no indication of foul play in that separate records issue or evidence connecting it to a data breach.

text: This article touches on something I've been ruminating about the past few months - the lack of control users have over their own security posture. Like many people, I use dozens of online applications a day, from banking through to childcare booking platforms to online shopping. With data breaches becoming ubiquitous and a common occurrence, providers are under pressure to secure their platforms. This means they're all attempting to implement "best practice", with various degrees of maturity and efficacy. The consequence of this is a huge degree of friction on a daily basis. Myriad authentication apps and schemes. Some using TOTP. Some using SMS 2FA. Some using push notifications through their own app. Some using magic links via email. Some with passwords, some without. Maintaining all these has become a significant administrative burden. But the enforcement, and inability to opt out, means I have limited say in choosing NY security posture for each service. Some accounts I have are throwaways that I couldn't care less if they were compromised. Even with strong and secure passwords, I still need 2FA. Worse, those that I do want a strong security posture with often have a backup recovery scheme, such as magic links via SMS, that I deem inherently insecure. Yet I am expected to trust that the platform provider knows what is best for me. As mentioned in the article, losing access to platforms has been a bigger issue for me than account compromise. For example, I had an old Twitter account I wanted to access once X took over. Although I had the password, they had implemented 2FA since the last time I logged in. Since In didn't have a current email on file with them, I couldn't receive the verification link and have now permanently lost access to that account. Providing that I had the (strong) password, that I was using the same static IP address I originally signed up with, and providing government identification was insufficient to regain control. I'm a fan of passkeys. I now also use a Yubikey. But simple passwords still have their place and can be useful and secure I'd handled well on both sides.

text: A "data breach" refers to unauthorized access to nonpublic or protected data. Scraping content that is publicly viewable without logging in - or even with logging in, since an account is effectively disposable - is not a "data breach" (as far as any typical usage of the term goes). In hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn, the 9th Circuit (US) ruled that scraping publicly accessible data does not violate the CFAA's "without authorization" clause (hiQ was bulk scraping public LinkedIn profile data - in violation of LinkedIn's ToS). The Supreme Court later specifically narrowed the CFAA in Van Buren v. United States saying "exceeds authorized access" applies to accessing areas of a system you aren't entitled to enter at all, not misusing access you legitimately have (regardless of ToS violations). Other CFAA cases have ruled similarly - being legitimately granted access (i.e. signing up for an account, or browsing publicly without logging in, since the site is intended to be available to the public) and then misusing it is not "hacking". So in the U.S., it's not a computer crime ("hacking"/"breach") to scrape data, and nobody uses the term "data breach" to refer to scraping publicly available data on a public site, except for apparently you.
